Total-, Alveolar and Dead Space Ventilation
Ventilation
Transfer of ambient fresh air into the lung is required for a continuous O2 and CO2 exchange between the
alveolar gas and pulmonary blood. Ventilation is described as movement of fresh air from ambient to alveoli,
where gas exchange occurs, and the subsequent movement of alveolar used air back to the atmosphere.
Therefore, ventilation is responsible for the refreshing of alveolar gas.
Total Ventilation, Dead Space Ventilation, and Alveolar Ventilation
For effective gas exchange, the air that we inhale must reach the alveolar surface. Before starting inspiration,
both the alveolar region and the conducting airways are filled with used air from a previous expiration (see
figure). As inspiration starts, the fresh breath pushes the used air from the dead space into the alveoli
replacing it with fresh air. Since our breath volume (VT) is normally much larger than dead space volume (VD),
most part of the fresh air also enters the alveoli (in this figure 300 ml). This portion of our VT entering the
alveoli is called alveolar volume (VA). Therefore, our tidal volume is the sum of dead space volume and
alveolar volume:
VT = VD + VA
(1) 
The number of breaths we take in one minute is called respiratory frequency (FR). Thus, the volume of air we
breathe in a unit of time (in a minute) is determined by multiplying the breath volume (VT) and respiratory
frequency (FR) and is called total ventilation (VE). Similarly, dead space ventilation (VD) and alveolar
ventilation (VA) are calculated as the product of FR and corresponding dead space and alveolar volumes:
therefore, ventilations are obtained by multiplying both sides of equation (1) by FR:
FR • VT = FR • VD + FR • VA
(2)
Thus:
Total ventilation VE = Dead space ventilation VD + Alveolar ventilation VA

Calculation of Physiological Dead Space using the Bohr Equation
Dead space volume is normally not accessible for direct volume measurement. Therefore, it can be indirectly 
calculated from fractional concentrations or partial pressures of O2 or CO2 in the inspired, alveolar and mixed 
expired gases, which can be sampled during breathing.  
Starting with expiration we first exhale the gas from the dead space followed by the gas coming from the 
alveolar region (see figure). Thus, our exhaled volume, VT, is composed of two gas volumes from different 
origins. One is VD carrying out fresh air from the dead space (no gas exchange occurs in dead space) and the 
other is VA (= VT – VD) carrying used alveolar gas. The gas fractions in these volumes are referred to as FI for 
dead space gas = inspired gas and FA for alveolar gas.  After mixing both volumes to VT by collecting them in a 
bag, the gas fractional concentration is referred as FE. 
We know from equation (1) that:  
VT = VA + VD
replacing VA by (VT – VD) results in: 
VT = (VT - VD)+ VD
Accounting for the amount of gases:
Total amount exhaled = amount exhaled with VA + amount exhaled with VD

Metabolic Rate
Cellular metabolism (the “fire of life”) consumes O2 and produces CO2 and
energy. Its minimal value is called Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), and is
influenced by body size and body temperature. BMR changes about 10% for
each 1° C change in body temperature.
This is important during fever or
hypothermia; e.g., The BMR of a patient with a body temperature of 38 C
(instead of 37 C) will be increased from 300 to 330 ml O2 / min. The BMR of a
patient with hypothermia (36 instead of 37 C) will be decreased from 300 to
275 ml/min. This effect of hypothermia has clinical applications in neuro and
cardiac surgery

Maximum Oxygen Uptake (VO2 max)
Adults consume about 300 ml of oxygen each minute (300 ml/min) during rest.
This value is increased in proportion to the workload during exercise and
reaches a maximum that is 10 times higher than the resting value and is
defined as maximum O2 uptake (VO2 max). Elite athletes in running or in other
aerobic events have even higher values of maximum O2 uptake.
CO2 Output (VCO2)
CO2 production in the body is linked to O2 consumption and is approximately
280 ml/min during rest and increases with increasing workload. CO2 is
eliminated from body only through ventilation in the lung.

Respiratory Exchange Ratio (R)
The ratio of CO2 output to O2 uptake is called the “respiratory quotient” (RQ) in
the tissues and “respiratory exchange ratio” (R) in the lungs.
When
carbohydrates are metabolized as in the example below RQ = 1.0.
C6H12O6 + 6O2 = 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy
R = RQ = VCO2/VO2 = 6CO2/6O2 = 1
When fats are metabolized, RQ = 0.7 (fasting metabolism). For most proteins,
RQ = 0.8.
During “steady state” (defined as normal quiet breathing at rest) RQ is equal to
R. This implies that pulmonary gas exchange exactly matches the needs of
metabolism in the peripheral tissues. However, RQ and R deviate from each
other in
the non-steady state conditions that occur during exercise, breathe
holding, crying, hyperventilation, hypoventilation, etc.

Partial pressure of gases in a gas mixture
All gas molecules of a gas mixture are moving randomly and producing collectively a total
pressure, which is dependent on altitude. At sea level this total pressure is 760 mm Hg
(called barometric pressure) and decreases with elevation. Each individual gas type
produces part of this total pressure in proportion to its fractional concentration in the mixture.
This is called partial pressure of this certain gas. For example, 21% of air is oxygen and
thus its partial pressure is 21 % of the total air pressure.
According to Dalton`s law:
PB = P1 + P2 + ----- + Pn + PH2O
PB is barometric pressure; P1,P2 and Pn are partial pressures of gas components and PH2O
is partial pressure of water.
The ideal gas law can be applied for one gas component as well as for the sum of all dry
gases of a gas mixture:
PX ∙ V = MX ∙ R ∙ T       applied for component x
(PB – PH2O) ∙ V = M ∙ R ∙ T     
applied for the sum of dry gases
Division of both above equations:
PX/(PB – PH2O) = MX/M = FX fraction of the gas X 
Rearrangement:
PX = FX ∙ (PB – PH2O)
The above equation enables you to calculate the partial pressure of any respiratory gas by the given
fractional concentration of the gas at a known barometric pressure.

Inspired air and inspired O2 partial pressure (PIO2)
Outside air consists of gases in a ratio of approximately 21% O2 (fraction 0.21) and 79% nitrogen
(fraction 0.79) with varying water vapor, depending on temperature and humidity of the air.
With
inspiration, outside air is heated to body temperature and humidified by evaporation from the airway
mucosa. After air reaches the more distal airways it is heated (37 ºC) and humidified (100% saturated at
37 ºC), and its water vapor pressure approaches 47 mm Hg. the inspired partial pressure of O2 (PIO2)
can be then calculated as:
Inspired PO2 = Inspired O2 fraction x (Barometric pressure – water vapor pressure)
PIO2 = PIO2 = FIO2 ꞏ (PB – PH2O)
= 0.21 ꞏ (760 - 47) = 0.21 x 713 = 150 mm Hg
and inspired N2 partial pressure as: 
PIN2 = 0.79 x 713 = 563 mm Hg
Please note that there are two factors that can significantly alter PIO2, namely barometric pressure (PB) 
and the inspiratory O2 fraction (FIO2).
PB depends on altitude and decreases with increasing altitude, whereas FIO2 is independent of altitude
and remains at 0.21 at any elevation. For example, PB decrease to 347 mm Hg at an altitude of 20,000
ft above sea level and consequently PIO2 at this altitude is:
PIO2 = FIO2 ꞏ (PB – PH2O)
= 0.21 ꞏ (347 - 47) = 0.21 x 300 = 63 mm Hg
FIO2 is changed when a healthy person or a patient is breathing supplemental O2. In such a case the 
O2 fraction of inspired gas is elevated. For example by breathing 60% O2 (FIO2 = 0.6) at sea level, the 
calculated PIO2 will be:
PIO2 = FIO2 ꞏ (PB – PH2O)
= 0.6 ꞏ (760 - 47) = 0.6 x 713 = 428 mm Hg

Alveolar PO2 (PAO2)
Alveolar PO2 (PAO2) is defined as partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolar gas and is
very important for the diffusion of O2 from alveolar gas into the capillary blood.
PAO2 is normally lower than PIO2, because oxygen is continually removed from
alveolar gas by the pulmonary capillary blood. On the other hand CO2 is added to the
alveolar gas from the blood. However, this addition of CO2 and removal of O2 are
linked to one another by the respiratory exchange ratio (R). When R=1, both are
equal and therefore the drop in PO2 (from PIO2 to PAO2) is equal to the rise in PCO2
(from PICO2 = zero to PACO2). Therefore:
PAO2 = PIO2 - PACO2
(1)
However, R is on average less than one which implies that CO2 production is a little
less than O2 consumption. The above equation is then corrected for this difference
between the two gases as:
PAO2 = PIO2 – (PACO2 / R)        (2)
Example: For the following set of given values:
PIO2 =147 mm Hg, PACO2 = PaCO2 = 40 mm Hg, and R = 0.8.
Alveolar PO2 will be:   PAO2 = 147 – (40/.8) = 147 – 50 = 97 mm Hg.

Alveolar PCO2 (PACO2) 
PACO2 is the CO2 partial pressure of alveolar gas and is nearly identical with
PCO2 of arterial blood (PaCO2).
Metabolic CO2 is added to the alveolar gas from the blood of pulmonary
capillaries and eliminated from the lung by alveolar ventilation. Therefore
PACO2 is linked to the balance between CO2 production and alveolar
ventilation. This relationship is illustrated in the following equation:
PACO2 = 863 x VCO2/VA
863 is a constant that results from applying partial pressures instead of
fractions and using a factor converting CO2 output (normally measured in
STPD) and alveolar ventilation (normally measured in BTPS) to the same
measuring conditions.
With normal values of:
•
CO2 output = 250 ml/min 
• Alveolar ventilation = 5400 ml/min
We obtain:
PACO2 = 863 x 250/5400 = 40 mm Hg

Definition of alveolar ventilation
Normoventilation:
Normal alveolar ventilation
e.g. PaCO2 normal (= 40 mmHg)
Hyperventilation:
Alveolar ventilation is increased in excess of
metabolic needs, therefore:
PaCO2 is reduced below normal (< 40 mmHg)
Hypoventilation:
Opposite of hyperventilation
e.g. PaCO2  is above normal (> 40 mmHg)
Hyperventilation: is defined as ventilation in excess of what is needed to maintain a normal PaCO2. As a
result, the arterial PCO2 is decreased. As shown in the Figure 1, doubling alveolar ventilation from 5 to 10
L/min reduces the PaCO2 from 40 to 20 mm Hg. A PaCO2 < 40 mm Hg in a patient indicates
hyperventilation. The cause of hyperventilation can be aspirin toxicity, high altitude hypoxia,
progesterone (pregnancy), anxiety, and a metabolic Acidosis.
Hypoventilation: is defined as ventilation not adequate to maintain a normal PaCO2. As a result the
alveolar and arterial PCO2 are increased.
If CO2 output is constant and alveolar ventilation is halved,
from 6 to 3 L/min, then PaCO2 will double, from 40 to 80 mm Hg. A PaCO2 > 40 mm Hg in a patient
indicates hypoventilation.
The cause may be primary; e.g., barbiturate overdose or secondary as a
compensation for metabolic alkalosis.
Hyperpnea: is defined as increased ventilation without changes in PCO2 (= normal) as in exercise.
Tachypnea: is defined as breathing with an increased respiratory frequency
Effect of Exercise: Ventilation increases during exercise, but this is not hyperventilation. The alveolar 
ventilation increases exactly the right amount to keep arterial PCO2 at the normal value of 40 mm Hg.  
This increase in alveolar ventilation is needed to eliminate the increased amount of CO2 production during 
exercise. For example, if CO2 production is doubled during exercise, then the alveolar ventilation would 
also double to eliminate the excess CO2 production, but arterial PCO2 remains unchanged at 40 mm Hg. 
Hyperventilation (decreased PaCO2) will occur during exercise only if the exercise intensity crosses the 
anaerobic threshold and lactic acid is produced which in turn stimulates breathing in excess of what is 
needed for elimination increased CO2 production. 
Alveolar–arterial PO2 difference (A-a)PO2
(A-a)PO2 is the PO2 difference between alveolar gas and arterial blood. In a healthy person this difference
is small (3 to 10 mm Hg) and is caused by normal anatomical shunts (see pulmonary circulation) as well
as diffusion problems and mismatching of ventilation and perfusion in the lung. This (A-a)PO2 increases
significantly in diseases that enhance shunting or V/Q mismatch. The (A-a)PO2 will be discussed in more
detail in the lecture on mechanisms of hypoxemia.

KEY CONCEPTS
1. Alveolar ventilation is the volume of fresh (non–dead 
space) gas entering the respiratory zone per minute. It 
can be determined from the alveolar ventilation equation, 
that is, the CO2 output divided by the fractional 
concentration of CO2 in the expired gas. 
2. The concentration of CO2 (and therefore its partial 
pressure) in alveolar gas and arterial blood is inversely 
related to the alveolar ventilation. 
3. The anatomic dead space is the volume of the 
conducting airways. 
4. The physiologic dead space is the volume of lung that 
does not eliminate CO2. It is measured by Bohr's method 
using arterial and expired CO2. 
5. The two dead spaces are almost the same in normal 
subjects, but the physiologic dead space is increased in 
many lung diseases.
